terms.plain: Water lost to the air and to crop growth
terms.text: The water that leaves a field as vapour: evaporation from the soil plus the water plants draw up and release through their leaves. A crop that used 800 mm of ET needed 800 mm of water from rain, irrigation and what was already in the soil. In this tool, ET for a field comes from OpenET, which estimates it from Landsat satellite images and weather data.

The water a well-watered, mown grass surface would use in that day's weather. It depends only on sun, heat, humidity and wind, not on your crop. Hot, dry, windy days have a high reference ET. Multiplying it by a crop coefficient (a number that says how much of that a given crop uses at each stage) gives the crop's water demand.

A number from about 0 to 1 calculated from red and near-infrared light reflected by the field. Bare soil reads around 0.1 to 0.2; a dense, healthy canopy reads 0.8 or more. It shows how much green leaf is present. It does not measure soil health, yield or organic matter, and it stops rising once a canopy is dense.

How wet or dry the top few centimetres of soil are compared with what is usual for that month. Zero is normal; -1 or lower is clearly drier than usual; +1 or higher is clearly wetter. It comes from NASA's SMAP satellite, whose pixels are about 9 km wide, so it describes the valley around the field rather than the field itself, and it sees only the surface, not the root zone.

terms.plain: How long the frost-free season is
terms.text: The number of days between the last frost of spring and the first frost of autumn, and how much that changes from year to year. Warm-season crops such as teff die at the first frost, so the tool checks in how many of the last 30 years the frost-free season was long enough for each crop.

Rainfall minus reference ET over a month or year. A strongly negative number means the weather demands far more water than rain supplies, so crops depend on irrigation. It is a pressure gauge, not proof that a crop was short of water.

terms.plain: Crop water demand minus usable rain
terms.text: What irrigation has to supply: the crop's water demand minus the part of rainfall the crop can actually use. It is the amount the crop needs, not the amount you pump: pumping is higher because no system is 100 % efficient.

terms.plain: A wide view from far away vs a sharp view of one spot
terms.text: A satellite sees everywhere, repeatedly and for free, but indirectly: it measures reflected light or microwaves and a model turns that into rainfall, moisture or water use, averaged over a pixel that may be 30 m or 9 km wide. A rain gauge, soil probe, flow meter or well measures the real thing, but only at one point. They are strongest together. Example from this valley: NASA's weather grid put the frost-free season at about 134 days; after correcting it with a station-informed dataset it is about 81 to 93 days, which is the difference between teff being safe and teff being a gamble.

terms.plain: How much to trust a score
terms.text: High: several independent sources for this field agree. Medium: based on satellite or weather-model data for this field, without ground confirmation. Low: based on general crop tables or on something this tool cannot see (prices, pests, herbicide history, your water right). A low-confidence score is a question to take to a local adviser, not an answer.

terms.plain: How the overall score is built
terms.text: Each rotation gets a score from 0 to 1 on each of your priorities. Your sliders set how much each priority counts. The overall score is the weighted sum. Change the sliders and the ranking changes: there is no single best rotation, only the one that fits your priorities best.

disclaimer: This tool supports your decisions. It does not replace your own judgment or local agricultural expertise.
limits: Field outlines are detected from satellite images, not surveyed.
The crop history comes from a satellite crop map and can be wrong for single years.
Water figures are estimates of crop demand, not measurements of what you pumped.
No prices, yields, costs, pests, herbicide history or water rights are known to the tool.
Soil data are survey map units, not samples from your field.
